summary:
Malacca is one of the thirteen states of Malaysia and stands under the Malaysian national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", which covers oral and anal sex for any person regardless of gender, consent or privacy, with a maximum of twenty years' imprisonment and whipping; sodomy was first criminalised in 1871, and the provisions are not confined to Malaysian citizens and have been applied to foreign nationals. A visitor to Malacca who is neither a citizen nor a Muslim is exposed to the federal Penal Code alone.

Section 377D of the Penal Code, "outrages on decency", criminalises gross indecency in terms the Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile, last updated in 2024, describes as usable to target transgender people. The same profile records evidence of the law being enforced in recent years, a crackdown on the LGBT community since the 2018 election, a high-profile 2021 case in which a prominent transgender woman fled the country following threats of arrest, and consistent reports of discrimination and violence, with transgender people particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but that is prosecutorial discretion rather than legal protection.

The Sharia layer applies only to Muslims. Every one of the thirteen states, together with the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, alongside liwat and musahaqah, with penalties reaching three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. State Islamic religious departments carry out enforcement, and the enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, so the boundary between compliant and offending presentation is set by officers on the ground.

Human Rights Watch, in a report published 10 August 2022 with the Malaysian group Justice for Sisters, documents government-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people across Malaysia. It cites the federal penal code provisions of up to twenty years for oral and anal sex and the Sharia codes in Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya that typically criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, and it details conversion and rehabilitation programmes, officials shutting down events, and the 2021 prosecution of the transgender woman Nur Sajat in the western state of Selangor. Its finding is that pervasive antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity influences law enforcement, judicial outcomes, family behaviour and public discourse.

Violence against transgender people is documented and largely unpunished. A trans woman was killed in Klang in June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months. Arbitrary arrest is likewise documented over decades, including repeated arrests of individual women more than twenty times, a mass arrest of sixteen trans women at a wedding in June 2014, and a pattern of strip-searches and sexual assault by religious officials during detention. In July 2020 the Federal Territories Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his full licence to carry out enforcement against transgender persons; the International Commission of Jurists demanded the order be revoked.

Criminal exposure extends to social venues. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were published; seventeen civil servants identified among the arrestees were suspended. A magistrate rejected the request to extend remand on the ground that no case had been made out under 377B, yet release was delayed and more than 130 detainees were still being held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice for Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid. On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister said the provisions would be revisited; within days police raided another sauna in Penang. Earlier venue raids include a Kuala Lumpur gay bar in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants in 2022, and eleven shopping malls in May 2023 over the sale of Pride watches.

Identity documents are controlled by the state. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes, and a 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holding that sex is determined at birth and unaffected by reassignment surgery was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity in one's gender; that judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented marker change is historical: in 1975 the Registration Department recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti permitted her to marry under Sharia law.

There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors. The nearest documented statement of entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay, and a warning to gay foreign ministers not to bring their partners. Same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable; Mahathir told the Cambridge Union in June 2019 that Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage, and no political party pursues LGBTQ legal reform.

Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. Sharia courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months and may order cross-dressing and other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months in some states, extended to a year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment.

Legal challenges have failed to remove the framework. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional. The Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and sixteen Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, but on federalism grounds about which legislature may enact the offence, not on the substance, and nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern is national rather than local: thirteen states plus two federal territories maintain comparable Sharia offences, and documented raids cluster in major urban centres such as Kuala Lumpur, Penang and Klang rather than in any single state. Malacca should be read against that pattern, not as an outlier with its own record.

Discretion has moved with political pressure. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon, but the same provisions produced a gay bar raid in August 2018, an LGBTQ Halloween party raid in 2022, mall raids over Pride merchandise in May 2023, and the Chow Kit sauna raid of 28 November 2025; a Home Minister's undertaking on 2 December 2025 to revisit the provisions was followed within days by a further sauna raid in Penang.

Foreign nationals are drawn into proceedings. In the Chow Kit raid 31 of the more than 130 detainees still held were foreign nationals whose embassies intervened, and section 377B applies regardless of citizenship. A prominent transgender woman left the country in 2021 rather than face arrest, indicating flight as a practical response to threatened prosecution.

The comparison points cited by monitors are domestic rather than international: the 2021 prosecution of Nur Sajat in Selangor and the conversion and rehabilitation programmes documented by Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters in August 2022.

The Registration Department's routine rejection of gender-marker changes has been sustained since the 2016 Kuala Lumpur High Court ruling was overturned on appeal in 2017.

Residents face employment consequences as well as charges: seventeen civil servants were suspended after being identified among the 208 men arrested in the November 2025 raid, and reporting on killings of trans women has been marked by investigative attitudes that leave police mistreatment and impunity unexamined.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents a specific enforcement action, arrest or prosecution under section 377A, 377B or 377D within Malacca state itself; the raids, prosecutions and killings cited are recorded in Kuala Lumpur, Penang, Klang and Selangor. Whether Malacca's own Sharia enactment uses wording identical to the other twelve states is not stated by these sources, only that all thirteen maintain such offences.

The exact current penalties set by Malacca's Sharia enactment are not sourced here; the three-year term, RM5,000 fine and six strokes of caning are given as the ceiling across state enactments generally.

No source records how Malacca's religious department has used its powers against transgender residents in a defined period, and no Malacca-specific figure for arrests is available in this inventory.

Whether the Human Dignity Trust profile's reference to evidence of enforcement in recent years includes Malacca is unresolved; the profile is a national country profile without a state-level breakdown.
